title: Prices and consumer rights in Mauritius
summary: The goods whose prices the Government fixes and what they cost today: bread, ration rice, flour, cooking gas, petrol and diesel. The goods with a capped mark-up, what a price tag must show, your rights when you buy, and where to complain. Checked on 20 November 2026.
audience: Anyone who shops in Mauritius and wants to know what a thing should cost, what the shop owes them and who to call.

sections.heading: Which prices does the Government fix?

blocks.text: The Government fixes the price of bread, ration rice, flour, cooking gas, petrol and diesel. The Consumer Protection (Price and Supplies Control) Act lets the Minister fix the price of listed goods by regulations, and makes it an offence to sell above it. The Ministry of Commerce and Consumer Protection uses three systems: a maximum price, a maximum mark-up and a maximum recommended retail price.

The State Trading Corporation, the Government's trading arm, imports all petroleum products and cooking gas, and supplies ration rice and flour. It says the Government fixes all its selling prices. Rice and flour are sold below their landed cost, and a subsidy makes up the difference.

blocks.text: The Ministry's list of maximum fixed prices also shows onions and potatoes at Rs 50 a kilo and iodised table salt at Rs 3.00 for 125 g. The list is undated. The prices in the table are for Mauritius and Rodrigues alike.

sections.heading: How are petrol and diesel prices set?

blocks.text: A Petroleum Pricing Committee sets them under regulations of 2011, using average world prices over six months: the last three and the next three. Both fuels rose three times in 2026. Petrol went from Rs 58.45 to Rs 64.25 on 16 April, to Rs 70.65 on 15 August and to Rs 77.70 on 29 September. Diesel went from Rs 58.95 to Rs 64.80 on 25 March, to Rs 71.25 on 16 April and to Rs 78.35 on 29 September. At the last review the calculated increase was about 18%, but the regulations capped it at 10% because the Price Stabilisation Account was in deficit.

The Corporation publishes what makes up the price. Of the Rs 77.70 for a litre of petrol, Rs 10.13 is VAT at 15%, Rs 9.87 is excise duty, Rs 7.20 is a contribution to the subsidy on cooking gas, flour and rice, and Rs 3.00 is the retail margin of the filling station.

sections.heading: Which goods have a capped mark-up?

blocks.text: For about thirty kinds of goods the Ministry does not fix a price but limits the percentage a trader may add. Its list for the island of Mauritius includes milk powder at 24%, infant milk powder at 17%, edible oil at 22%, pulses at 24%, basmati and long grain rice at 20%, canned fish at 20%, pasta at 25%, baby diapers at 23%, butter and margarine at 28%, and sanitary pads at 20%. Pharmaceutical products have a regressive maximum mark-up. Rodrigues has its own list, with separate wholesale and retail percentages.

sections.heading: What must a price tag show?

items: Every trader must put a label on a specimen of the goods showing the selling price. It must say that the amount includes VAT, or that VAT is zero or nil.
The label is placed close to the goods, in Mauritian rupees.
A trader may not sell above the price on the label. If more than one price is displayed at once, you pay the lowest.
A trader who refuses to sell goods on display at the displayed price commits an offence. So does one who gives a misleading indication of price.
An announced price reduction must show the prior price, meaning the lowest price charged in the 30 days before. Perishable goods are excepted.
A trader is not bound by an obvious and inadvertent error, once it is corrected and the buyer is told.

Since 1 July 2026 the label on 21 kinds of pre-packed goods, among them rice, flour, edible oil, milk powder, sugar, pulses and detergents, must also show the unit price for a kilogramme or a litre. The letters MRP mark a maximum retail price and SP a fixed subsidy.

blocks.text: Failing to label a price is an offence that can bring a fine of up to Rs 500,000. For listed offences an officer or a police officer serves a fixed penalty notice, payable at the District Court within 21 days.

sections.heading: What are your rights when you buy something?

blocks.text: The Ministry's advice page states two. Goods must be of satisfactory quality: the standard a reasonable person would accept, given the description and the price, and free from defects unless these were pointed out at the time of sale. And goods must be as described, on the packaging, on a display notice or by the seller. Its consumer guide of 2024 lists eight consumer rights, among them the rights to safety, to information, to choose, to be heard and to redress.

A manufacturer's guarantee comes on top of these statutory rights, and the Ministry says a trader should not discourage you from using them. Ask for the guarantee certificate with all its conditions in writing, and keep every receipt. When you buy a second-hand car from an authorised dealer, the Ministry tells you to check that it carries a warranty of at least 2 months, covering faulty parts, labour and materials.

If you buy on hire purchase or credit, the Ministry tells you to read the contract before signing and to obtain a receipt for any deposit, a copy of the signed contract and a schedule of repayments. To cancel, give the trader written notice by registered post.

sections.heading: Where and how do you complain?

items: Tell the seller first, in writing if you can, as soon as possible, and keep a copy. If you phone, note the date, the time and the name of the person you spoke to.
If that fails, contact the Consumer Affairs Unit of the Ministry of Commerce and Consumer Protection: hotline 185, office line 460 2500, the MOPRI mobile application or the Citizen Support Portal.
The Unit handles complaints, checks trade premises and tries to settle disputes between traders and consumers by mutual agreement. In case of deadlock the matter goes to court.

blocks.text: If you cannot find ration rice, the State Trading Corporation set up a complaints line in September 2026: 5944 3434, on weekdays from 9 am to 4 pm.
